meta.note: Coordinates marked confidence=approximate are rounded to the site area, not an exact address. Many sites are private property, structurally unsafe or actively patrolled. This dataset documents them; it is not an invitation to enter.
meta.accessNote: Access ratings are an assessment from each site’s ownership, status and press coverage — they are not verified on the ground and they change. "No known security" is not permission: entering private property without it is trespass, and many of these buildings are structurally unsafe regardless of who is watching.
meta.scope: Only places that are actually abandoned. Buildings still in everyday use are not listed, even when they have been damaged, and neither are sites that have been demolished away to nothing. Where part of a site has been converted and is lived in, the entry says so.
meta.imageNote: Photographs come from Wikimedia Commons and are reproduced under the licence shown with each one. Credit links go to the file page, which carries the full licence terms. Some are of a surviving detail rather than the main building, and a few predate the damage described.

sites.name: Ayr Station Hotel
sites.summary: B-listed 1880s railway hotel, empty for years. Fire in May 2023, then a major blaze on 25 September 2023 that closed Ayr station and the rail line. South Ayrshire Council carried out emergency partial demolition; the owner's attempt to block it failed in 2024. The remaining shell is still unresolved.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Ayr Station Hotel fire
sites.accessNote: Council-controlled demolition site with a standing cordon around the shell.

sites.name: Sauchiehall Street derelict block
sites.summary: Three-storey derelict building in Glasgow city centre went up around 01:36 on Tuesday 1 September 2026. Nine appliances, one height appliance and three specialist resources attended. Roads closed, no injuries reported.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene: hoardings, cordon and contractor security.

sites.name: Princes Street disused building
sites.summary: A large fire engulfed a disused building on Princes Street in the early hours of 9 July 2026. The site was earmarked for hotel conversion. Transport across central Edinburgh was disrupted for days.
sites.sourceName: Bloomberg
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene on a main city street, cordoned and watched.

sites.name: Union Corner, Union Street
sites.summary: Major fire on 8 March 2026 in the Union Corner building at Union Street and Gordon Street in central Glasgow, a long-vacant commercial block near Central Station.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Union Street fire
sites.accessNote: Recent fire scene, hoarded and cordoned in the city centre.

sites.name: Strathmartine Hospital
sites.summary: Former psychiatric hospital closed in 2003. The site has become one of Dundee's worst hotspots for deliberate fire-raising, with repeated blazes across the abandoned wards over two decades.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service
sites.accessNote: Known arson hotspot, so the site is watched and reported on.

sites.name: Bangour Village Hospital
sites.summary: Edwardian 'colony plan' psychiatric hospital opened 1906 — dozens of separate villas, a church and its own railway. Closed 2004 and left to rot; probably Scotland's best-known urbex site. Fire and vandalism have hit several villas.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Site security during redevelopment; the best-known urbex target in Scotland, so it is actively watched.

sites.name: Hartwood Hospital
sites.summary: Once the largest mental asylum in Europe with around 2,500 patients. Closed in the late 1990s, partially burned down and now severely unstable — collapsed floors and open roofs throughout the twin-towered main block.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Fenced. Collapsed floors and open shafts make it one of the most dangerous ruins in the country.

sites.name: St Peter's Seminary, Cardross
sites.summary: Brutalist Category A-listed seminary by Gillespie, Kidd & Coia, opened 1966, abandoned by 1987. Repeatedly vandalised and burned. Widely called Scotland's most important modern ruin; multiple restoration schemes have failed.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: The Kilmahew woodland around it is walkable, but the building itself is fenced off.

sites.name: Gartloch Hospital
sites.status: Hospital core derelict, estate is housing
sites.summary: Victorian asylum with a distinctive clock tower, closed 1996. The land around it was built out as housing and people live there now; the listed hospital core itself stayed empty, was gutted by fire and remains a shell behind hoardings.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: The former estate around it is a lived-in housing development.

sites.name: Lennox Castle Hospital
sites.summary: 1837 castle that became a hospital for people with learning disabilities, closed 2002. Gutted by fire in 2008 and again since. The roofless shell sits behind the Celtic FC training ground.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Woodilee Hospital
sites.status: Listed fragments derelict, rest is housing
sites.summary: Barony Parochial Asylum, opened 1875, closed 2000. Almost all of it has been cleared and replaced by housing that is lived in today — what is left on the map here is the handful of listed buildings that were never converted and are still empty and decaying.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: Most of the site is an occupied housing estate.

sites.name: Sunnyside Royal Hospital
sites.summary: Scotland's first purpose-built asylum (founded 1781, this site from 1858), closed 2011. Large listed complex near Montrose, vacant and on the at-risk register while conversion plans stall.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Craig Dunain Hospital
sites.summary: Inverness District Asylum, opened 1864, closed 2000. Part of the complex was converted into flats that are lived in; the section wrecked by a major fire while the building stood empty was never rebuilt and is still a burnt-out ruin.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: The converted blocks are occupied flats.

sites.name: Argyll and Bute Hospital, Lochgilphead
sites.summary: The last of Scotland's Victorian psychiatric asylums still in use, finally closed in 2017. Now a listed building awaiting a future.
sites.sourceName: Carte Urbex

sites.name: Mavisbank House
sites.summary: Category A-listed 1720s Palladian villa by William Adam, gutted by fire in 1973 and left open to the sky for fifty years. A long-running poster child for the Buildings at Risk Register; a rescue project finally started in the 2020s.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Active conservation project — scaffolded working site.

sites.name: Cambusnethan Priory
sites.summary: 1820 Gothic Revival mansion near Wishaw, a hotel and then a medieval-banquet venue before fires in the 1980s left it roofless. Category B-listed and among the most-photographed derelicts in Lanarkshire.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Crawford Priory
sites.summary: Extravagant Gothic country house near Cupar, abandoned since the 1970s. Roof gone, walls progressively collapsing; sections have come down in recent storms.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Private estate. Masonry has come down in recent storms.

sites.name: Buchanan Castle
sites.summary: Seat of the Dukes of Montrose, a WWII military hospital (Rudolf Hess was treated here), then stripped of its roof in 1954 to avoid tax. The shell has stood open ever since.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt

sites.name: Dunmore Park House
sites.summary: 1820s Tudor-Gothic mansion near Airth, abandoned and unroofed since the 1960s–70s. Next to the famous Dunmore Pineapple. Steadily losing masonry.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Dunalastair House
sites.summary: Baronial mansion near Kinloch Rannoch, used to billet Polish troops in WWII and derelict ever since. Now a genuinely dangerous ruin with collapsing floors.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt
sites.accessNote: Private land, and genuinely dangerous — floors have gone.

sites.name: Broadford Works
sites.summary: Category A-listed linen mill complex, one of the oldest surviving iron-framed mills in Britain. Closed 2004, hit by fire while vacant and repeatedly broken into as redevelopment plans drag on.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Glenmavis Distillery
sites.summary: Bathgate distillery closed in the early 20th century. Surviving listed ranges are roofless and overgrown, long-standing entries on the at-risk register.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Arichonan Township
sites.summary: Abandoned after the 1848 clearance, when residents resisted eviction and were tried in Inveraray. Stone walls and gables still stand on the hillside above Loch Sween.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt

sites.name: Badbea Clearance Village
sites.summary: Cliff-top settlement on the Caithness coast built by families cleared from inland straths. Conditions were so exposed that children and livestock were reportedly tethered. Last resident left in 1911.
sites.sourceName: Travelness

sites.name: Fearn Airfield
sites.summary: Scotland’s single largest vacant and derelict site at 386 hectares. Built in 1941 as an RAF airfield and later a Royal Navy air station, it has been derelict for at least four decades — runways, dispersals and hangar bases still readable from the air.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Working farmland over most of the 386 ha.

sites.name: Fendom Airfield, Tain
sites.summary: RAF weapons range and wartime airfield opened in 1941 on the Dornoch Firth. Derelict by 1980 at the latest; 295 hectares of it, making it the third-largest derelict site in the country.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Farmland and MOD range land adjoin the site.

sites.name: Baldoon Airfield (RAF Wigtown)
sites.summary: RAF Wigtown closed in 1948 and has been left alone ever since. As recently as 2017 the site still held its control towers, hangars, two runways and fourteen abandoned air raid shelters across 184 hectares.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Farmland; the surviving structures are on private ground.

sites.name: Edzell Airbase
sites.status: Airfield derelict, part is an industrial estate
sites.summary: A WWI airfield that became RAF Edzell and then a US Navy Cold War listening station with a huge circular antenna array. The Americans left in 1997. A corner of it now trades as an industrial estate; the runways, bunkers and abandoned base buildings across the remaining 170 hectares do not.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Part of the site is now a working industrial estate.
sites.partlyOccupied: Part of the site is a working industrial estate.

sites.name: RAF Machrihanish
sites.status: Base buildings derelict, airfield still operational
sites.summary: NATO forward base on the Kintyre peninsula with one of the longest runways in Europe, built to take heavy transports and rumoured to have hosted US special forces. The RAF left in 1997. The runway is still flown from and part of the site trades as a business park, but the hardened shelters, bunkers and accommodation blocks are abandoned.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia
sites.accessNote: The airfield is still operational and MOD land adjoins it.
sites.partlyOccupied: The runway and a business park are in use; MOD land adjoins.

sites.name: RAF Aird Uig / Gallan Head
sites.summary: Cold War radar station on the westernmost headland of Lewis, decommissioned in 1958 and progressively abandoned. Empty accommodation blocks and radar platforms sit above the cliffs; the headland has since passed to a community trust.
sites.sourceName: Gary Gough — RAF Aird Uig
sites.accessNote: The headland is community-owned with public access; the buildings themselves are not maintained.

sites.name: RAF Milltown
sites.summary: Airfield north-east of Elgin on the Moray Firth. Flying stopped in 1977 and it carried on as a communications station before winding down; runways, dispersals and antenna bases remain across the flat coastal ground.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Ardeer Explosives Works
sites.summary: Alfred Nobel opened his dynamite factory on the Ardeer sands in 1871 — at its peak the largest explosives works in the world, with thousands of staff and its own railway. A small operational plant survives at one end; the other 331 hectares of blast mounds, blockhouses and buried magazines have been derelict since 2005.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Parts of the wider site are still operational chemical works with real security.
sites.partlyOccupied: Parts of the wider site are still a working chemical plant.

sites.name: Bogside, Irvine
sites.summary: The other half of the Nobel Industries empire on the Ayrshire coast, plus a former racecourse. Derelict since 2005 and, at 221 hectares, the sixth-largest abandoned site in Scotland.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland

sites.name: Port of Ardersier
sites.status: Yard derelict, port redevelopment under way
sites.summary: Oil-platform fabrication yard opened in the early 1970s on the Moray Firth, employing thousands through the North Sea boom. Closed in 2001 and empty for two decades; work has since started on turning it into an operational port, so parts of the 254-hectare site are a live construction project rather than a ruin.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Being redeveloped as an operational port; manned security.
sites.partlyOccupied: An active port redevelopment with staff on site.

sites.name: Powharnel opencast mine, Muirkirk
sites.summary: Opencast coal mine abandoned in 2013 when Scottish Coal went into liquidation, leaving the restoration bond nowhere near enough to fill the void. 245 hectares of unrestored workings — one of the scandals of the Ayrshire coalfield.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Open moorland, but unrestored opencast voids and flooded pits.

sites.name: Benbain opencast mine
sites.summary: Another East Ayrshire opencast left unfinished by the 2013 collapse of Scottish Coal. 193 hectares of spoil and open void that were supposed to be returned to farmland.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland
sites.accessNote: Open moorland with unrestored opencast voids.

sites.name: Strathmore railway line
sites.summary: The old main line through Strathmore, closed to passengers in 1967 under the Beeching cuts and to freight in the early 1980s. 165 hectares of abandoned trackbed, cuttings, bridges and shuttered station buildings.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — largest vacant and derelict sites in Scotland

sites.name: Hirta, St Kilda
sites.summary: Britain’s most remote inhabited place until the 36 remaining islanders asked to be taken off. On 29 August 1930 the Harebell carried them to the mainland, ending over 2,000 years of habitation. They left a plate of oats and an open Bible in each cottage. Now a double UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Hirta
sites.accessNote: National Trust for Scotland. Landing is possible by boat in summer, subject to their rules.
sites.partlyOccupied: A defence radar station and NTS staff are based on the island in season.

sites.name: Mingulay
sites.summary: Island at the southern tip of the Outer Hebrides where around 30 families lived by crofting, fishing and fowling on 200-metre sea cliffs. Conditions and isolation beat them and the last left in 1912. The village street of roofless houses still stands above the bay.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Mingulay
sites.accessNote: National Trust for Scotland; landing by boat, weather permitting.

sites.name: Swona
sites.summary: From the early 1930s a single family, the Rosies, were the only people on this Pentland Firth island. In 1974 the last brother and sister sailed off, leaving the house and their cattle behind. The cattle were never collected and their descendants still run wild there — a feral herd studied by scientists.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Swona
sites.accessNote: Privately owned island with a feral cattle herd. No landing without permission.

sites.name: Stroma
sites.summary: Island in the Pentland Firth whose population peaked at around 375 in the early 1900s. As families left, the school, shop and ferry became unviable and the community collapsed; the last residents went in 1962. A harbour finished just as the island emptied is still there.
sites.sourceName: The Scotsman — Nine abandoned islands of Scotland
sites.accessNote: Privately owned but access is not obstructed; boat landing only.

sites.name: Inchkeith
sites.summary: Fortress island in the middle of the Firth of Forth, fortified from the 16th century and heavily built up with gun batteries and barracks in both World Wars. The garrison left after 1945 and the lighthouse was automated in 1986; the tunnels, emplacements and empty blocks have been derelict ever since.
sites.sourceName: The Sunday Post
sites.accessNote: Privately owned island. Tunnels and gun emplacements are unlit and unmaintained.

sites.name: Hallaig, Raasay
sites.summary: Township on the east side of Raasay cleared in the 1850s, its people shipped to Australia. Immortalised in Sorley MacLean’s poem "Hallaig", probably the best-known Gaelic poem of the 20th century. Only stone footings and a memorial cairn remain.
sites.sourceName: Travelness

sites.name: Rosal Township, Strathnaver
sites.summary: One of the townships burned out in the Sutherland Clearances of 1814 by Patrick Sellar’s men. Excavated in the 1960s and now an interpreted trail in Strathnaver — the clearest surviving plan of a pre-Clearance Highland settlement.
sites.sourceName: Historic Environment Scotland
sites.accessNote: Interpreted trail on Forestry and Land Scotland ground.

sites.name: Tureen Street School
sites.summary: Yellow ashlar board school in Calton, finished in 1875 and one of the oldest surviving school buildings in Glasgow. Long closed, windows boarded, and listed on the Buildings at Risk Register while conversion schemes come and go.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.accessNote: Boarded and monitored while conversion schemes are considered.

sites.name: Holmlea Primary School
sites.summary: Edwardian red sandstone board school in Cathcart, closed in the 2000s and left empty. Repeatedly broken into and vandalised while housing conversion plans stalled.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Fern School
sites.summary: Late-19th-century rural primary school. Funding cuts in the 1990s cut rolls until it closed in the mid-2000s; it has stood empty ever since, with desks, books and coat pegs still in place — a well-known urbex time capsule.
sites.sourceName: Obsidian Urbex Photography
sites.accessNote: Private rural property; no known active security, which is why the interior survived.

sites.name: Former Inverkeithing Primary School
sites.summary: The town’s old primary school stood empty after pupils moved to a new building, and was gutted by a large fire that brought Scottish Fire and Rescue crews out in force — the classic fate of a vacant Scottish school.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Fire and Rescue Service

sites.name: Tirfergus House
sites.summary: Kintyre country house near Campbeltown, abandoned in the second half of the 20th century and now a roofless shell being taken apart by weather and vegetation.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Rosslynlee Hospital
sites.summary: Midlothian District Asylum of 1874, latterly a psychiatric hospital, closed around 2011. The listed main block with its tower has stood empty and open to the weather since, with periodic vandalism and small fires.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Kingseat Hospital
sites.status: Admin block and villas derelict, rest converted
sites.summary: Aberdeen District Asylum, built on the same villa-colony plan as Bangour and opened in 1904, closed in the mid-1990s. Some villas became private houses and are occupied; the administration block and the villas nobody bought were left to rot and burn.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland
sites.partlyOccupied: Several villas are now private homes.

sites.name: Clune Park Estate
sites.accessNote: Council demolition site with contractor security; the tenements are structurally unsafe.
sites.summary: Around 430 flats in 45 tenement blocks, built after WWI by the shipbuilders Lithgows to house their workforce. Derelict since 1997 and steadily emptied — under 20 people were left by 2019. The press christened it "Scotland’s Chernobyl". A £31m clearance scheme began demolishing it in 2025, starting with the church and school.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Clune Park Estate

sites.name: Govanhill Picture House
sites.status: Auditorium derelict, shops at street level
sites.partlyOccupied: A grocer and a fabric shop trade from the ground floor.
sites.accessNote: Occupied at street level; the auditorium above is closed off.
sites.summary: Egyptian-themed cinema of 1926 seating 1,200 — one of only a handful of Egyptian-style picture houses left in Britain. Films stopped in 1961 and it went through bingo and warehouse use. B-listed and on the at-risk register; re-roofed in 2012 to stop it collapsing. Shops occupy the frontage while the auditorium sits empty.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Lyceum Cinema, Govan
sites.summary: Streamlined 1938 super-cinema on Govan Road by McNair and Elder, seating around 2,600. Split into a bingo hall and cinema in 1974 and eventually closed altogether. B-listed, boarded and slowly rotting on one of Govan’s main streets.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Bon Accord Baths
sites.accessNote: Held by a restoration charity; access is by their arrangement, not by walking in.
sites.summary: Art deco swimming baths of 1940 in Justice Mill Lane, where Olympic champion David Wilkie learned to swim. Closed by the council in 2008 during budget cuts and empty since. The pool hall, diving boards and terrazzo are still in place under a leaking roof; a community charity is trying to reopen it.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Whitevale Street Public Baths
sites.summary: Victorian public baths and steamie in Dennistoun, opened 1902, with a pair of tall Italianate towers that still dominate Whitevale Street. Closed and boarded for decades, the pool hall open to the sky in places.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Church Street School swimming pool
sites.summary: Listed Victorian school swimming pool in Partick, used as a public facility until it closed in 1997. It has been on the Buildings at Risk Register continuously since 1999 — one of the longest-standing entries on it.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia

sites.name: Lion Chambers
sites.accessNote: Netted and hoarded on a busy city-centre street because the concrete is shedding.
sites.summary: Eight-storey tower of 1907 on Hope Street, one of the earliest reinforced-concrete buildings in Britain — walls only four inches thick, built that way to fit a tiny plot. Category A-listed and empty since the 1990s. Repeatedly named among the most endangered buildings in Scotland; the cost of fixing the concrete has defeated every scheme so far.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Glenwood Centre, Glenrothes
sites.summary: One of the new town’s neighbourhood shopping precincts — butcher, chemist, newsagent, grocer. The shops emptied as retail moved out of town, and the shell fell into disrepair and became a focus for crime and antisocial behaviour. Fife Council won compulsory purchase powers to clear it.
sites.sourceName: Fife Council

sites.name: Nithsdale Hall
sites.summary: Mission hall of 1887–88 on Nithsdale Drive in Pollokshields, burnt out in 2006 and left as a roofless shell behind hoardings ever since.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Shettleston Hall
sites.summary: The old burgh hall on Wellshot Road, built when Shettleston was still its own place rather than part of Glasgow. Long out of use, boarded and deteriorating.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Possil Railway Station
sites.accessNote: Sits beside a live railway — the line itself is not abandoned and entering it is an offence.
sites.summary: Station building on Balmore Road, closed to passengers in the Beeching era. The stone building survives at street level while the line below stayed in use for freight.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Sentinel Works
sites.summary: Engineering works off Jessie Street in Polmadie, part of the belt of south-side industry that emptied out from the 1970s. Roofs partly gone, yard overgrown.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: St Columba Episcopal Church, Clydebank
sites.summary: Episcopal church and hall in Clydebank, redundant and empty. One of the many Scottish churches emptied by falling congregations and left with no viable second use.
sites.sourceName: Derelict Glasgow

sites.name: Gates Rubber Factory, Heathhall
sites.accessNote: Called a death trap by the council; floors and roofs are unsound.
sites.summary: Built in 1913 as the Arrol-Johnston car factory - an early reinforced-concrete daylight factory - then aircraft work in WWI and rubber production for Gates until it closed. Empty for decades and a magnet for arson, with two fires in 2017 alone. The council has drawn up developer guidance and demolition is on the table.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: George Hotel, Stranraer
sites.summary: Coaching hotel on the main street since the early 1800s, disused since 2007. Bought by the council in 2017 to deal with it; surveyors found the roof unrepairable, and demolishing a B-listed building needs Historic Environment Scotland to agree. It has sat boarded in the middle of town ever since.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: Mercury Inn Hotel, Moffat
sites.summary: Roadside hotel at the entrance to Moffat, empty for over twenty years. When The Ferret asked readers to nominate the worst eyesore in Dumfries and Galloway, this came top by a distance. A petition to demolish it was raised in 2011; the owner says restoration is coming.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: Rosefield Mills
sites.accessNote: Owned by a buildings trust doing stabilisation work.
sites.summary: Ornate Victorian tweed mill on the Nith, one of the grandest industrial buildings in the south of Scotland. Weaving stopped around the 1930s and the shell has stood ever since. Dumfries Historic Buildings Trust bought it in 2018 and is chasing funding to get a roof back on.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: 107-109 High Street, Dumfries
sites.summary: Georgian tenement of the 1820s standing empty on the main shopping street. Named in The Ferret survey as one of the buildings dragging the town centre down - the reporter found it occupied by nothing but dead pigeons. The owner has no plans to sell.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: Edingham Munitions Factory, Dalbeattie
sites.accessNote: Farmland and light industry now surround the surviving blocks.
sites.summary: Second World War cordite factory built on farmland outside Dalbeattie, employing thousands. Production stopped at the end of the war and the concrete blast walls, blockhouses and process buildings were simply left. Much of the layout is still readable across the fields.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: Creca Camp
sites.summary: Wartime camp near Annan, part of the vast munitions complex strung along the Solway coast. The huts and roads outlasted their purpose by eighty years and are now a scattering of concrete in the fields.
sites.sourceName: The Ferret — derelict buildings in Dumfries and Galloway

sites.name: Woodhead Lead Mine
sites.accessNote: Open hill ground above Carsphairn; the shafts are unfenced.
sites.summary: A whole mining village above Carsphairn - two rows of miners cottages, a smelt mill, a school and a manager house - built for the lead workings and abandoned when the mine closed in 1873. The gables and street plan still stand on the moor.
sites.sourceName: Travels with a Kilt

sites.name: Craigendoran Pier
sites.accessNote: The rotting timbers are the hazard here, not a fence.
sites.summary: The North British Railway built this pier in 1882 so trains could hand passengers straight onto the Clyde steamers, and for ninety years it was how Glasgow got to the coast. Steamer services were withdrawn in 1972. The timber piles and decking have been collapsing into the firth ever since, a mile east of Helensburgh.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Craigendoran

sites.name: Cardross Old Parish Church
sites.accessNote: Stands openly in the village; the shell itself is fenced off.
sites.summary: On the night of 5–6 May 1941 Luftwaffe bombers aiming for the Clyde shipyards hit Cardross village, killing three people and wrecking the parish church. It was never rebuilt. The tower and roofless walls still stand in the middle of the village and serve as its war memorial.
sites.sourceName: St Mahew, Cardross

sites.name: Kilmahew Castle
sites.accessNote: In the Kilmahew woodland, which is walkable, but the walls are unstable.
sites.summary: Tower house of the Napiers in the wooded glen above Cardross. Parts of the south and west walls were rebuilt in the 19th century with the idea of turning it into a modern mansion, but the work was abandoned half-finished. It shares the estate with St Peter’s Seminary and with the site of Kilmahew House, which burned in 1995 and was demolished.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Kilmahew Castle

sites.name: Portkil Battery, Kilcreggan
sites.accessNote: Caravans and sheds now share the ground; the emplacements are open and unlit.
sites.summary: Built between 1900 and 1904 on Fort Road to cover the sea approach to Clydeside, armed with two 6-inch and two 4.7-inch quick-firing guns. The 6-inch guns were taken out in 1916 and the rest in 1928, and the battery never returned to service. Emplacements, magazines and observation posts survive and are listed.
sites.sourceName: Secret Scotland

sites.name: Woodbank House, Balloch
sites.accessNote: Boarded and fenced, and most of the roof has gone.
sites.summary: Georgian mansion on Luss Road at the foot of Loch Lomond, on land settled since 1670 and renamed Woodbank when a Glasgow merchant bought it in 1774. It ran as a hotel from the 1930s until it closed in 1981 and has been rotting ever since, with council and owners each failing to act. It carries a 1981–85 start date on the government derelict register.
sites.sourceName: Geograph — Woodbank House

sites.name: Killearn Hospital
sites.accessNote: On private ground in Blane Wood; concrete ward blocks and roads survive under the trees.
sites.summary: One of five emergency hospitals the government built across Britain in 1940 for the war casualties it expected, put up on requisitioned land beside the ruins of Killearn House. It carried on afterwards as a neurosurgical hospital and was abandoned in 1972. The single-storey ward blocks and their connecting corridors are still in the woods.
sites.sourceName: Secret Scotland

sites.name: Arrochar Torpedo Range
sites.summary: Torpedo testing station at the head of Loch Long, where weapons were fired down the loch and recovered. The deep, straight, sheltered water made it ideal, and it ran for decades before closing in the early 2000s. The pier, workshops and slipway sit on the government derelict register.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Royal Ordnance Factory, Bishopton
sites.partlyOccupied: Part of the wider estate is being built out as housing.
sites.accessNote: The derelict blocks are fenced within an active redevelopment.
sites.summary: One of the largest explosives factories in Britain, opened in 1937 and spread across square miles of Renfrewshire with its own railway network and hundreds of blast-separated buildings. Production wound down through the 1990s. Forty-three hectares remain on the derelict register — blast mounds, cordite blocks and roads going nowhere.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Torryburn Hotel, Kintore
sites.accessNote: Fenced off in the middle of a village; the structure is unsound.
sites.summary: Georgian coaching hotel on Gauchill Road, gutted by fire in 2015 and never touched since. The burnt shell has stood in the middle of Kintore for a decade while the site sits on the government derelict register.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal

sites.name: Archaeolink Prehistory Park, Oyne
sites.accessNote: Privately marketed land; the turf-roofed buildings are open and unmaintained.
sites.summary: A whole museum left to the weather. Archaeolink opened in 1997 as an award-winning prehistory park below Bennachie, with a grass-roofed visitor centre buried into the hillside and full-scale reconstructions of an Iron Age farm and a Roman marching camp. Visitor numbers never covered the running costs and it shut in 2011. Thirteen acres of it have been on the market ever since.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal

sites.name: Coutens Farm, Oldmeldrum
sites.accessNote: Working farmland surrounds it; the steading roofs have collapsed.
sites.summary: Farmhouse and steading abandoned by 2001 and left to fall in. Roofs down, trees through the windows, the yard swallowed by vegetation — the ordinary kind of Scottish dereliction that never makes the listed-building registers.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal

sites.name: Mathers Factory, Inverurie
sites.summary: Meat processing works on Harlaw Road. The company was liquidated in 2016 and the plant stopped in 2017, leaving an empty warehouse and its car park behind the trading estate.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal

sites.name: Stoneywood Paper Mill
sites.summary: Paper has been made on the Don at Stoneywood since 1770, and for two centuries the mill was one of the biggest employers in Aberdeen. It went into administration in September 2022 with the loss of hundreds of jobs, and the site was added to the derelict register soon after.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: Rubislaw Quarry
sites.accessNote: Fenced. A 140-metre vertical drop into deep water — the single most lethal site on this map.
sites.summary: The hole Aberdeen came out of. Granite was cut here from 1740 until 1971, and most of the Granite City is built from it — 140 metres deep and about 120 metres across. It filled with water after the pumps stopped and has sat as a private, fenced-off lake ever since, on and off the market for years.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: St Margaret of Scotland Chapel and Convent
sites.accessNote: Boarded in a busy street in Old Aberdeen; the owners have said nothing about plans.
sites.summary: Chapel with an attached convent on The Spital, shut for around twenty years and on the Buildings at Risk Register. Aberdeen City Council lists it among its derelict sites; the owners have stayed silent about what happens next.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Palmerston Road Fishworks
sites.summary: Smokehouses and fish-processing sheds behind the harbour, three of them Category C-listed, empty since the 2000s and on the Buildings at Risk Register. What is left of the trade that made Aberdeen before oil did.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Logie Stores
sites.summary: A shopping arcade built to serve the Middlefield housing scheme, long emptied of tenants and repeatedly broken into and vandalised. It caught fire in September 2025.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: Gordon Centre, Bridge of Don
sites.summary: A campus of Aberdeen College on Corunna Road, closed in 2011 when teaching moved elsewhere. It has stood empty ever since with no use found for it.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: Victoria Road School, Torry
sites.summary: Granite board school in Torry, closed in 2011 and empty since. It went to auction in September 2025 after more than a decade on the council derelict list.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: Dunbar Halls, Old Aberdeen
sites.summary: University of Aberdeen halls of residence beside St Machar, emptied around twenty years ago and never brought back. The blocks still stand while the university keeps reconsidering what to do with that end of the campus.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: Hilton Outdoor Sports Centre
sites.accessNote: Fenced off by the council.
sites.summary: Sports pavilion at Stewart Park, shut after a fire more than a decade ago and never repaired. The putting green and tennis courts around it have gone back to grass behind the fencing.
sites.sourceName: The Press and Journal — Abandoned Aberdeen

sites.name: The ABC, Kirkcaldy
sites.summary: Opened in 1906 and running as a cinema for most of the century, the B-listed ABC closed in December 2000 when ticket sales collapsed. It has stood shut on the High Street ever since, one of the longest-empty landmark buildings in Fife.
sites.sourceName: Buildings at Risk Register for Scotland

sites.name: Eastriggs MOD Depot
sites.partlyOccupied: Part of the rail yard was brought back into civilian use in 2024.
sites.accessNote: A former ammunition depot with its own railway and active operators on part of it.
sites.summary: The largest derelict site in Scotland at 430 hectares. Eastriggs began as part of HM Factory Gretna, the enormous First World War cordite works that ran for nine miles along the Solway and had its own town, railway and power station. It carried on as a Ministry of Defence ammunition depot until the stock was removed in 2009 and the depot wound up. Mile after mile of storage sheds, bunkers and rail sidings.
sites.sourceName: Secret Scotland

sites.name: Lyness Naval Base, Hoy
sites.partlyOccupied: The pumping station and one oil tank are now the Scapa Flow Museum.
sites.accessNote: Open ground on Hoy; the surviving structures are unmaintained.
sites.summary: The shore base for Scapa Flow, the anchorage of the Grand Fleet and then the Home Fleet. Up to 12,000 people were stationed in and around Lyness in the Second World War, and the base had cinemas, a power station and enormous buried oil tanks. Only a fraction of what stood here survives — foundations, roads and concrete across thirty-two hectares of hillside.
sites.sourceName: Undiscovered Scotland

sites.name: Montrose Airfield
sites.partlyOccupied: A heritage centre occupies a small part of the original station.
sites.accessNote: Farmland and industrial units cover much of the ground.
sites.summary: Britain’s first operational military airfield, opened by the Royal Flying Corps in 1913, a year before the war it was built for. It trained pilots through both world wars and closed in 1952. Fifty-two hectares sit on the derelict register — hangar bases, dispersals and the outline of the landing ground still legible from the air.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: RAF Dallachy
sites.accessNote: Farmland; the perimeter track and hardstandings are still in place.
sites.summary: Coastal Command airfield on the Moray Firth, home of the Dallachy Strike Wing whose Beaufighters hunted German shipping in the Norwegian fjords. It took heavy losses — the raid of 9 February 1945 is remembered as Black Friday. Closed after the war and returned to farmland, with runways, dispersals and the odd hut surviving across sixty-five hectares.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Bandeath Royal Naval Armament Depot
sites.partlyOccupied: An industrial estate uses part of the ground.
sites.summary: Naval armament depot on the Forth at Throsk, built in the First World War to load and store mines and shells, with a jetty on the river and its own rail network. It closed in the 1970s. Rows of blast-walled magazines stand in the fields beside a working industrial estate.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Barony Colliery, Auchinleck
sites.partlyOccupied: The A-frame headgear itself is a restored memorial in community care.
sites.accessNote: The memorial is publicly accessible; the surrounding derelict ground is not maintained.
sites.summary: A deep mine from 1907 that survived a disaster in 1962, when four men died and the shafts collapsed, and kept working until 1989. The pit buildings were cleared but the 1954 A-frame headgear was saved by a community trust and stands as a memorial to the Ayrshire coalfield — the last of its kind in Britain. Forty-four hectares around it remain derelict.
sites.sourceName: Wikipedia — Barony A Frame

sites.name: Westfield opencast site
sites.accessNote: A very deep, partly flooded void on private ground.
sites.summary: One of the deepest man-made holes in Europe. Westfield was worked for coal from the 1950s and went down over two hundred metres before the machines stopped in the late 1980s. Sixty-eight hectares of void and spoil have been on the derelict register ever since, through a run of failed schemes to fill or reuse it.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Comrie Colliery bing, Blairhall
sites.summary: Comrie was one of the last deep mines sunk in Scotland, opened in 1936 and closed in 1986. The colliery went, the bing stayed: sixty-one hectares of spoil north of Blairhall, still on the register forty years later.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Lanarkshire Steelworks, Motherwell
sites.summary: One of the Motherwell steelworks that went down in the collapse of the Lanarkshire iron and steel trade in the early 1980s, taking thousands of jobs with it. Thirty-seven hectares on Craigneuk Street have been derelict for forty years — longer than the plant’s last owners ran it.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Glengarnock Steelworks site
sites.summary: Iron and then steel was made at Glengarnock from 1841, and the works were the reason the village existed. Steelmaking ended in 1985 and the rolling mill soon after. Thirty hectares at Lochshore have stayed derelict since, the largest hole in the middle of any North Ayrshire town.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Crail Airfield (HMS Jackdaw)
sites.accessNote: Sold for agricultural use; the buildings are unmaintained and used for filming.
sites.summary: Commissioned as HMS Jackdaw in October 1940 and used to train torpedo-bomber crews on Swordfish and Albacores — the Luftwaffe rated it enough to put it in their target files. Closed in 1960 and sold as farmland, which is why it survived: hangars, the naval hospital and a torpedo trainer unlike anything left elsewhere still stand, along with the 1947 runways. The most complete 1940s Royal Naval Air Station anywhere in Britain.
sites.sourceName: Airfields of Britain Conservation Trust

sites.name: Stobs Military Camp
sites.status: Abandoned, best-preserved WWI camp in Britain
sites.accessNote: Farmland outside Hawick; an archaeology project works on the site.
sites.summary: An army training camp from 1903 that became an internment and prisoner-of-war camp in the First World War, holding around 6,000 German prisoners in some 200 huts. It served again in the Second World War and closed in the 1950s. Nothing else in Scotland combines a training camp, an internment camp and a POW camp on one site, and no other has standing buildings — huts, firing ranges and practice trenches survive across the moor.
sites.sourceName: Stobs Military Camp project

sites.name: Sutors of Cromarty coastal batteries
sites.accessNote: Reached on foot above the cliffs; the emplacements are unlit and unfenced.
sites.summary: Gun batteries on both headlands at the mouth of the Cromarty Firth, built to close the entrance to the fleet anchorage at Invergordon in the First World War and rebuilt for the Second. Emplacements, magazines, searchlight positions and observation posts are strung along the cliffs, abandoned since 1945.
sites.sourceName: Secret Scotland

sites.name: Turnberry Airfield
sites.partlyOccupied: The golf links were laid back over part of the airfield.
sites.summary: A flying school in the First World War and a Coastal Command operational training unit in the Second, built over the Turnberry golf links twice and given back twice. Runways and dispersals still cut across the course, and the memorial to the airmen killed here stands beside the fairways.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: RAF Crimond hospital camp
sites.summary: The hospital and accommodation camp for the naval air station at Crimond on the Buchan coast. The airfield went back to farming after the war and the camp was simply left — eight hectares of huts, foundations and roads at Moss Side.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Spittal of Glenshee Hotel
sites.accessNote: Open ruin beside the A93; structurally unsafe.
sites.summary: A drovers’ inn on the old road over the Cairnwell, latterly the hotel every skier heading for Glenshee knew. In August 2014 fifty firefighters fought a blaze that gutted it in the early hours. More than a decade on the ruins are virtually untouched and still falling apart beside the main road.
sites.sourceName: The Courier

sites.name: Belleisle House Hotel, Ayr
sites.accessNote: Fenced within a public park.
sites.summary: A late-18th-century Category B-listed mansion in Belleisle Park, run for years as a council hotel. In 2019 a workman’s blowtorch set the roof alight and the fire stripped the building back to a shell. South Ayrshire Council has had it on the market ever since.
sites.sourceName: Ayrshire Post via inkl

sites.name: Manor Park Hotel, Monkton
sites.summary: Roadside hotel on the Kilmarnock road at Monkton, beside Prestwick airport. It stopped trading and went onto the council derelict register in 2022.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Parkstone Hotel, Prestwick
sites.summary: Seafront hotel on Esplanade at Prestwick, one of the string of resort hotels built when the Ayrshire coast was where Glasgow went on holiday. Empty and on the derelict register since 2021.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Newton Hotel, Dumfries
sites.summary: Hotel on the Glasgow road out of Dumfries, closed and derelict since the early 1990s. Thirty years on the register and counting.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Whitehouse, Lamlash
sites.summary: A hotel and grounds above Lamlash Bay on Arran, empty since the early 2000s. At 4.6 hectares it is the largest derelict hospitality site on the register.
sites.sourceName: Scottish Vacant and Derelict Land Survey

sites.name: Queen Victoria Works, Dundee
sites.summary: When it finally stopped in 1990 this was the oldest working jute mill in the world, in the city jute built. The mills around it became flats, offices and a museum; Queen Victoria Works was left empty and has gone downhill fast ever since.
sites.sourceName: Secret Scotland
